labs.title: Responsible LLM Use Readiness
labs.intro: Score your organization from 1 to 5 on seven dimensions of responsible LLM use to see your profile on a radar chart. Start your 90-day plan with the weakest dimension.

dimensions.name: Use-case clarity
dimensions.question: How clearly have you identified LLM use cases with owners, baselines and a defined picture of good output?
dimensions.low: Run a short workshop to list text-heavy tasks and pick one pilot with an owner and a measured baseline.
dimensions.high: Keep a scored use-case register and review it quarterly against measured results.

dimensions.name: Data protection and privacy
dimensions.question: How well do you control which data may be used with LLMs and meet PIPEDA or provincial privacy obligations?
dimensions.low: Classify your data, confirm vendor terms on training use, retention and location, and run a simple privacy assessment for your first use.
dimensions.high: Embed privacy assessments into every new AI use and audit vendor terms and logs each year.

dimensions.name: Acceptable-use policy
dimensions.question: Do staff have a clear, current policy on approved tools, data rules and their responsibility for outputs?
dimensions.low: Publish a two-page acceptable-use policy with a traffic-light data rule and an approved business tool.
dimensions.high: Review the policy regularly, track acknowledgements and update it with lessons from real use.

dimensions.name: Prompt and output quality
dimensions.question: How consistently do teams use structured prompts, shared templates and review of outputs?
dimensions.low: Create a shared prompt library starting with three tested templates for frequent tasks.
dimensions.high: Assign owners to key templates and version them as tasks and models change.

dimensions.name: Evaluation
dimensions.question: Do you test LLM use cases against fixed test sets and rubrics before and after changes?
dimensions.low: Build a 20-item test set and a simple rubric for your pilot and record a baseline score.
dimensions.high: Re-run evaluations automatically on every prompt, document or model change and monitor live samples.

dimensions.name: Security
dimensions.question: How well are prompt injection, data leakage and tool permissions controlled in your LLM uses?
dimensions.low: List what each LLM tool can read and change, and require human approval for any action it takes.
dimensions.high: Test new integrations with adversarial prompts and review access and action logs routinely.

dimensions.name: Staff literacy
dimensions.question: How well do staff understand LLM strengths, limits, prompting and the rules for safe use?
dimensions.low: Run a hands-on session on real tasks for all staff and name a champion in each team.
dimensions.high: Grow champions into a community of practice and include AI literacy in onboarding.

exam.q: A sales manager asks a chat assistant for a competitor's current price list and gets a detailed, confident table. What should she conclude?
opts: Chat assistants are always updated with current prices
The prices are accurate because the model sounded confident
The model searched the competitor's private systems
The table may be invented and must be verified against a real source
exam.why: LLMs generate plausible text and can hallucinate specifics such as prices unless grounded in a verified source.

exam.q: Which training stage mainly turns a base model into an assistant that follows requests such as 'summarize this memo'?
opts: Pre-training on more web text
Instruction tuning on examples of requests and good responses
Reducing the context window
Raising the temperature
exam.why: Instruction tuning teaches the model to treat input as a request and respond helpfully; pre-training alone produces a base model.

exam.q: Roughly how many tokens would a 1,500-word English document use, using the course's rule of thumb?
opts: About 15,000 tokens
About 150 tokens
About 1,000 tokens
About 2,000 tokens
exam.why: With roughly 100 tokens per 75 words, 1,500 words is about 2,000 tokens, though the exact count varies by model.

exam.q: A long chat about a project starts giving answers that ignore instructions given early in the conversation. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
opts: The context has grown long or been truncated; start a fresh chat with a clean, complete prompt
The model is tired; wait an hour
The temperature is too low; raise it
The provider has deleted the account
exam.why: Long histories fill the context window and can push out or dilute earlier instructions. A fresh, well-structured prompt resets the context.

exam.q: For a task that extracts invoice numbers into a spreadsheet, which combination is best?
opts: Free-form prose output reviewed occasionally
High temperature and a short prompt
Low temperature, defined fields, a missing-value rule and validation
Asking the model to guess missing invoice numbers
exam.why: Structured extraction needs consistency and explicit handling of missing data, plus checks before data enters systems.

exam.q: A team member writes the prompt 'Make this better' with a pasted customer letter. Which missing element would most improve results?
opts: The model's version number
A request to use more adjectives
The audience, purpose and desired format of the improved letter
A longer greeting to the model
exam.why: Context, task and format tell the model what 'better' means; without them it must guess.

exam.q: Which technique most reliably improves consistency for a classification prompt?
opts: Including a few labelled examples of each category
Asking the same question in capital letters
Removing the category definitions to shorten the prompt
Using a different model for each request
exam.why: Few-shot examples show the model the exact pattern wanted, which typically improves consistency.

exam.q: A manufacturer wants an assistant to answer questions from its 200 work instructions. Testing shows correct answers for some machines but mix-ups between similar presses. What is the best fix?
opts: Ask operators to stop asking about presses
Fine-tune the model on general manufacturing textbooks
Increase the temperature
Add metadata such as machine ID to document chunks and filter retrieval by it
exam.why: Mix-ups between similar documents are a retrieval problem; metadata and filtering help the system fetch the right source.

exam.q: A consultancy wants its proposals drafted in its house style. It has a style guide and a few good examples. What should it try first?
opts: Fine-tuning a model before trying anything else
A structured prompt including the style guide and sample sections
Building a private data centre
Using the highest temperature available
exam.why: Style can usually be achieved with prompting and examples; fine-tuning is reserved for cases where prompting and RAG have been measured and fall short.

exam.q: What is the main trade-off of running an open-weight model on your own infrastructure?
opts: More control over data and deployment, but you take on hosting, security and maintenance
No responsibility for security at all
It always costs less and performs better than any closed model
It removes the need to evaluate outputs
exam.why: Self-hosting open-weight models gives control and portability while shifting operational responsibilities to you.

exam.q: A health-services SME is choosing an LLM provider. Which question is most important to answer in writing first?
opts: Which celebrity endorses the product?
What colour scheme does the app use?
Will our data be used for training, how long is it retained and where is it processed?
How many employees does the provider have?
exam.why: Data use, retention and location terms determine whether the service can be used with sensitive information.

exam.q: An LLM email classifier processes 500 emails a day for 20 days. Each request uses 1,000 input tokens and 20 output tokens. How many input tokens are used per month?
opts: 1 million
10 million

exam.q: Which change typically reduces token cost the most for a RAG assistant without lowering quality?
opts: Asking for longer answers
Sending fewer, more relevant retrieved chunks per question
Keeping all past conversations in every request
Switching to the largest available model
exam.why: Retrieved context is often the largest share of input tokens; better retrieval cuts cost and can improve focus.

exam.q: Before launching an LLM tool that drafts quote follow-up emails, the team wants evidence it works. What should they build?
opts: Nothing, because the provider has already tested the model
A slide deck showing the best demo output
A survey asking staff whether they like AI
A fixed test set of real examples and a rubric with an agreed pass threshold
exam.why: A test set and rubric give repeatable, comparable evidence specific to your task.

exam.q: An LLM assistant summarizes web pages for staff. A page contains hidden text telling the assistant to email the summary to an outside address. What is this?
opts: Prompt injection
Fine-tuning
Temperature drift
Tokenization
exam.why: Prompt injection is when content the model reads contains instructions that try to override the intended behaviour.

exam.q: A RAG assistant lets any employee retrieve passages from payroll files. Which control is missing?
opts: A higher temperature setting
A larger context window
Retrieval that respects existing document access permissions
More examples in the prompt
exam.why: The retrieval index should enforce the same access rights as the source systems to prevent data leakage.

exam.q: Under PIPEDA's limiting collection principle, how should an SME use personal information in LLM prompts?
opts: Personal information is never permitted in any business system
Include all available customer data for better context
Include only what the task needs and de-identify where possible
Collect extra data in case it is useful later
exam.why: Limiting collection means using only the personal information necessary for the identified purpose.

exam.q: Which item belongs in an SME's acceptable-use policy for LLMs?
opts: A rule that the user reviews and is responsible for any output they use
A guarantee that AI output is always correct
A requirement to use personal accounts for client work
A ban on reporting AI mistakes
exam.why: Human responsibility for outputs is a core element of a practical acceptable-use policy.

exam.q: A distributor is choosing its first LLM pilot. Which candidate best fits the selection criteria?
opts: Using the model to calculate monthly payroll deductions
Letting the model set credit limits for new customers
Having the model negotiate contracts directly with suppliers
Classifying incoming emails into order, quote, complaint or other for staff to route
exam.why: Email classification is frequent, easy to check and low harm; the others involve high-stakes decisions or exact calculation.

exam.q: Three months into adoption, staff in one team still avoid the approved LLM tool. Which response best reflects good change management?
opts: Mandate usage targets with penalties
Find their concerns, then provide hands-on coaching on their own tasks through a team champion
Remove the tool from all teams
Assume they will eventually adopt it without support
exam.why: Change models such as ADKAR emphasize understanding concerns and building knowledge and ability on real work, with reinforcement.

figures.title: The five building blocks of a prompt
figures.caption: Click each layer, from the bottom up, to see what it adds to a prompt that gets a usable first draft.

layers.label: Role
layers.text: Tell the model who to act as, such as an experienced customer service lead at a distributor.

layers.label: Context
layers.text: Give the background: audience, situation, relevant policy or data, and any constraints.

layers.label: Task
layers.text: State exactly what to do with a clear verb, including what to avoid.

layers.label: Format
layers.text: Specify length, tone and structure, such as three headings or a table.

layers.label: Examples
layers.text: Show one or more samples of good output; showing is often clearer than describing.

figures.title: How a RAG answer is produced
figures.caption: Watch questions move through the steps, then click 'Fix the bottleneck' to see why document quality decides RAG results.

steps.label: User question
steps.text: A staff member asks something like 'What is the lockout sequence for press 4?'

steps.label: Search documents
steps.text: The system searches the indexed company documents for passages that match the meaning of the question.

steps.label: Retrieve passages
steps.text: The few most relevant chunks are selected, ideally filtered by metadata such as equipment or site.

steps.label: Build the prompt
steps.text: Passages are added to the prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite the source.

steps.label: Answer with sources
steps.text: The model writes the answer with references the person can open and check before acting.

config.fix_text: Clean the document library first: remove duplicates and old versions, make files text-searchable and add metadata such as equipment and date.

figures.title: The LLM evaluation cycle
figures.caption: Click each stage to see what it involves, and notice that the cycle restarts whenever the prompt, documents or model change.

stages.label: Build test set
stages.text: Collect 20 to 50 real, de-identified examples, including messy and edge cases.

stages.label: Define rubric
stages.text: Agree criteria such as accuracy, completeness, format, tone and safety, and a pass threshold.

stages.label: Run and score
stages.text: Run every test item through the current prompt and model and score each output.

stages.label: Human review
stages.text: People who know the work check accuracy and tone and look for new failure modes.

stages.label: Improve
stages.text: Change one thing, such as the prompt, examples or retrieval, then re-run the whole set.
